title: Emerging International Best Practices for AI Model Specs
content:
Emerging International Best Practices for AI Model Specs
Words by: Edward Kembery, Nathan Lambert, Robert McCarthy, Jinge Wang, Peng Xu, Naying Hu, Clement Neo, Xu Jia, Miro Pluckebaum, Seán S. ÓhÉigeartaigh, Sören Mindermann, Christoph Winter, Lujain Ibrahim, Yawen Duan, Saad Siddiqui
Abstract
Frontier AI developers from around the world have begun to publish documents that describe how their AI models are intended to behave. Although these ‘model specifications’—or ‘model specs’, for short—are increasingly important in AI development and governance, little independent guidance exists for writing them.
This paper addresses this gap in five main sections. First, we outline the advantages of writing a model spec for AI developers and society at large. Second, we introduce a taxonomy for model specs that developers can take inspiration from. Third, we propose guidance for writing and implementing a spec in practice. Fourth, we note eight open problems related to writing model specs for safe and desirable behaviour.
We conclude with recommendations for frontier AI companies, governments, and research and civil society organisations.

report.summary: A new international research paper maps emerging best practices for AI 'model specs'—documents defining how models should behave—offering a taxonomy, drafting guidance, and eight open problems for frontier developers and regulators.
report.background: Since OpenAI published its Model Spec in May 2024, Anthropic's constitutional documents and Chinese labs such as DeepSeek have released similar behaviour guidelines, model specs have moved from internal design notes to public governance artefacts. They describe how a model should prioritise instructions, handle conflicts, refuse requests and behave in edge cases—effectively the 'intended behaviour' contract behind post-training and evaluation. Yet publication has been uneven: formats, scope and levels of detail vary wildly, few companies explain how specs are enforced, and no independent benchmark exists for what a good spec contains. Meanwhile regulators—the EU AI Act's GPAI code of practice, Singapore's safety frameworks and various national safety institutes—increasingly expect documented, auditable behaviour commitments. The paper, authored by researchers across institutions in the UK, US, China, Singapore and Europe, is an attempt to consolidate that fragmented landscape into shared international guidance before practices harden.
key_points: A model spec is a public or internal document stating how a model is intended to behave: how it resolves conflicting instructions, what it refuses, its tone, and its limits. The paper argues specs help developers align training and evaluation, reduce ambiguity, and give users, auditors and regulators something concrete to check behaviour against.

The authors propose a taxonomy of specs—differing in scope, level of abstraction, audience and whether they cover only the model or the surrounding product and deployment. This gives developers a menu of design choices rather than a single template, reflecting how diverse current published specs are.

Practical guidance covers drafting and implementation: writing testable principles, connecting spec clauses to evaluations and red-teaming, versioning, publishing change logs, and assigning internal ownership so the spec is a live engineering document rather than marketing copy.

Eight open problems remain unresolved, including how to handle value conflicts across cultures, how to make specs verifiable, how to govern updates, and how to prevent specs from becoming performative commitments disconnected from actual model behaviour.

Recommendations target three groups: frontier companies should publish substantive, testable specs; governments should avoid mandating rigid formats but require disclosure and auditing; researchers and civil society should build independent evaluations of whether models actually follow their stated specs.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this signals a shift from unilateral, company-specific behaviour documents toward shared expectations, with transparency about intent becoming a de facto norm and a potential procurement requirement. Developers gain a reference architecture for turning vague safety principles into testable clauses linked to evals and post-training data—useful for startups that lack policy teams. Regulators get a vocabulary for demanding auditable behaviour commitments without dictating values. For regular users, the payoff is clearer, comparable statements about what an assistant will and will not do, and stronger grounds to challenge systems that deviate. The main risk is 'spec-washing': polished documents that are neither enforced nor independently verified, which the paper's emphasis on verification aims to counter.
report.tools: Follow OpenAI's published Model Spec, Anthropic's constitution, and DeepSeek's model spec as reference examples. Watch SAIF's research output, Nathan Lambert's Interconnects newsletter, and evaluation tooling such as UK AISI's Inspect framework and third-party auditors like Meridian Labs' Petri for testing whether models follow their stated behaviour. Reading the full paper is the best starting point for teams drafting their own spec.
